newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu to visit Gabon Wednesday, army fights back.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu to visit Gabon Wednesday, army fights back.

text.p: Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko, under pressure to quit as rebels close in on Kinshasa, will travel to Gabon for an African mini summit on Wednesday and return to his capital two days later, a spokesman said.
With Laurent Kabila's rebels building up for a final push against Kinshasa, Zaire's government said its forces had counter-attacked and were battling to retake Kikwit.

On the humanitarian front, 1,200 Rwandan Hutu refugees who were to be airlifted home arrived safely by train in Zaire's third city of Kisangani -- the first such trip since 92 were killed in a stampede on Sunday.
"It is confirmed that the president will go to Libreville on Wednesday and will return on Friday. He is attending a meeting of heads of state," Mobutu spokesman Kabuya Lumuna told Reuters.
"The meeting is linked to the international mediation on Zaire," Kabuya said.
Kabila's rebels, who have said they are less than 85 km (50 miles) from Kinshasa, appealed for government troops to surrender to avert a bloody takeover of the capital.
However government forces said they had launched a counter-attack against the rebel forces.

"We are in the process of retaking Kikwit. Intense fighting is taking place. The rebels have lost 500 men," emergency rule prime minister Likulia Bolongo's military adviser, Captain Aime Atembina, told a news conference in Kinshasa.
Independent sources confirmed a belated counter-offensive but said the clashes were near Kenge, closer to Kinshasa.

Rebel radio said the rebels had ringed the airport outside Kinshasa and were about to take the whole city. There was no independent confirmation and a Reuters journalist in the area said there was no sign of rebel troops.
Diplomatic sources say the front line is close to the strategic Kwango River bridge 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.

South African Vice-President Thabo Mbeki and U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson held talks in Pretoria on ways to avert a battle for Kinshasa. Mbeki later announced plans to visit Zaire and five other nations in the region to keep peace talks on track.
U.N. agencies stepped up security precautions in Kinshasa, evacuating the last handful of non-essential staff, a senior U.N. source said.
A government statement said Mobutu was to have talks in Gabon with the presidents of Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon in Libreville.
It said the talks were a follow-up to a weekend peace summit between Mobutu, Kabila and South Africa's Nelson Mandela on a South African ship in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire.

A Mobutu aide said it would be wrong to interpret the president's departure as a flight into exile, recalling that the 66-year-old president, now suffering from prostate cancer, has always said he will not flee.
The rebel campaign to oust Mobutu, who has ruled for 32 years, began last October.
Many Kinshasa residents openly welcome the prospect of Kabila's arrival but fear Mobutu's soldiers will again loot and pillage before fleeing.
In Paris, longtime Mobutu ally France expressed deep concern over rebel threats to take Kinshasa by force if necessary and renewed its appeals for a peaceful transition.
